danish.title: Sjette bog (1808–10) — Kapitel 26
paragraphs: Midt på sommeren modtog fyrstinde Mária et uventet brev fra fyrst Andrej i Schweiz med mærkelige og overraskende nyheder. Han meddelte hende sin forlovelse med Natásha Rostova. Hele brevet åndede kærlig henrykkelse over hans forlovede og øm og tillidsfuld hengivenhed for hans søster. Han skrev, at han aldrig havde elsket, som han gjorde nu, og at først nu forstod og vidste han, hvad livet var. Han bad sin søster tilgive, at han ikke havde fortalt hende om sin beslutning, da han sidst besøgte Lysye Gory, skønt han havde talt med sin far om det. Det havde han ikke gjort af frygt for, at fyrstinde Mária skulle bede faderen om at give sit samtykke, hvorved hun ville irritere ham og måtte bære hovedvægten af hans mishag uden at nå sit mål. »Desuden,« skrev han, »var sagen dengang ikke så endeligt afgjort, som den er nu. Min far insisterede dengang på et års udsættelse, og nu er der allerede gået seks måneder, halvdelen af den periode, og min beslutning er fastere end nogen sinde. Hvis lægerne ikke holdt mig her ved badene, ville jeg allerede være tilbage i Rusland, men som det er, må jeg udsætte min hjemkomst i tre måneder. Du kender mig og mit forhold til far. Jeg ønsker intet af ham. Jeg har altid været og vil altid være uafhængig; men at gå imod hans vilje og vække hans vrede nu, da han måske kun har kort tid tilbage hos os, ville ødelægge halvdelen af min lykke. Jeg skriver nu til ham om det samme spørgsmål og beder dig vælge et godt øjeblik til at aflevere brevet og lade mig vide, hvordan han ser på hele sagen, og om der er håb om, at han vil samtykke i at forkorte fristen med fire måneder.«
Efter lange overvejelser, tvivl og bønner gav fyrstinde Mária brevet til sin far. Næste dag sagde den gamle fyrste roligt til hende:
»Skriv og sig til din bror, at han skal vente, til jeg er død... Det varer ikke længe — snart sætter jeg ham fri.«
Fyrstinden ville svare, men hendes far lod hende ikke komme til orde og råbte med stadig højere stemme:

»Gift dig, gift dig, min dreng!... En god familie!... Kloge folk, hva'? Rige, hva'? Ja, en dejlig stedmor lille Nikolaj får! Skriv og sig ham, at han kan gifte sig i morgen, hvis han vil. Hun bliver lille Nikolajs stedmor, og jeg gifter mig med Bourienne!... Ha, ha, ha! Han skal heller ikke undvære en stedmor! Blot én ting: der skal ikke flere kvinder i mit hus — lad ham gifte sig og bo for sig selv. Måske flytter du også hen til ham?« tilføjede han og vendte sig mod fyrstinde Mária. »I Guds navn, rejs! Ud i kulden... kulden... kulden!«

Efter dette udbrud talte fyrsten ikke mere om sagen. Men undertrykt vrede over sønnens kujonagtige opførsel fandt udtryk i hans behandling af datteren. Til sine tidligere påskud for ironi var der nu føjet et nyt — hentydninger til stedmødre og elskværdigheder mod mademoiselle Bourienne.
»Hvorfor skulle jeg ikke gifte mig med hende?« spurgte han sin datter. »Hun bliver en strålende fyrstinde!«

Og i den seneste tid bemærkede fyrstinde Mária til sin overraskelse og forvirring, at hendes far virkelig omgikkes mere og mere med franskmanden. Hun skrev til fyrst Andrej om modtagelsen af hans brev, men trøstede ham med håb om at forsone deres far med tanken.

Lille Nikolaj og hans opdragelse, broder Andrej og religionen var fyrstinde Marías glæder og trøst. Men ud over dette måtte enhver jo have personlige håb, og dybt i sit hjerte gemte fyrstinde Mária en skjult drøm og et håb, der udgjorde hendes livs største trøst. Denne trøstende drøm og dette håb blev givet hende af Guds folk — de halvtossede og andre pilgrimme, der besøgte hende uden fyrstens vidende. Jo længere hun levede, jo mere erfaring og iagttagelse hun fik af livet, des mere undrede hun sig over menneskers kortsynethed, der søger nydelse og lykke her på jorden: slæber, lider, kæmper og skader hinanden for at opnå den umulige, indbildte, syndige lykke. Fyrst Andrej havde elsket sin kone, hun døde, men det var ikke nok: han ville knytte sin lykke til en anden kvinde. Hendes far protesterede, fordi han ønskede et mere fornem og rigere parti for Andrej. Og de kæmpede og led og plagede hinanden og skadede deres sjæle, deres evige sjæle, for at opnå goder, der kun varer et øjeblik. Ikke blot ved vi dette selv, men Kristus, Guds Søn, kom ned til jorden og fortalte os, at dette liv kun er for et øjeblik og er en prøve; og alligevel klynger vi os til det og tror at finde lykke i det. »Hvordan kan det være, at ingen indser dette?« tænkte fyrstinde Mária. »Ingen undtagen disse foragtede Guds folk, som med ransel på ryggen kommer til mig ad bagdøren, bange for at blive set af fyrsten — ikke af frygt for hans mishandling, men af frygt for at bringe ham til at synde. At forlade familie, hjem og al verdslig velfærd for at vandre uden at klynge sig til noget, i hørgarnskittel fra sted til sted under et falsk navn, uden at skade nogen, men bedende for alle — for dem der jager én bort såvel som for dem der beskytter én: højere end det liv og den sandhed findes der ikke!«

Der var én pilgrim, en stille, koppearret lille kvinde på halvtreds ved navn Theodosia, som i over tredive år havde vandret barfodet og båret tunge lænker. Fyrstinde Mária holdt særlig meget af hende. En gang, da de sad i et rum med en lampe, der brændte svagt foran ikonen, og Theodosia fortalte om sit liv, kom den tanke pludselig med en sådan styrke til fyrstinde Mária, at Theodosia alene havde fundet livets sande vej, at hun besluttede selv at blive pilgrim. Da Theodosia var faldet i søvn, tænkte fyrstinde Mária længe over dette og besluttede til sidst, at hun, hvor mærkeligt det end måtte forekomme, måtte drage på pilgrimsfærd. Hun betroede denne tanke til ingen andre end sin skriftefader, pater Akínfi, munken, og han billigede hendes hensigt. Under påskud af en gave til pilgrimmene havde fyrstinde Mária forberedt et komplet pilgrimsudstyr til sig selv: en grov særk, bastsko, en ru frakke og et sort hovedtørklæde. Ofte, når hun nærmede sig kommoden med denne hemmelige skat, standsede fyrstinde Mária og tøvede, om tiden ikke allerede var kommet til at sætte sin plan ud i livet.

Ofte, når hun lyttede til pilgrimmenes fortællinger, blev hun så grebet af deres enkle tale, som var mekanisk for dem, men for hende så fuld af dyb mening, at hun flere gange var på nippet til at forlade alt og flygte hjemmefra. I fantasien så hun sig allerede ved Theodosias side, klædt i grove pjalter, vandrende med en stav, en ransel på ryggen, ad den støvede vej fra det ene helgensted til det næste, fri for misundelse, jordisk kærlighed eller begær, og omsider nående det sted, hvor der ikke mere er sorg eller suk, men evig glæde og salighed.

»Jeg kommer til et sted og beder der, og før jeg når at vænne mig til det eller komme til at holde af det, vandrer jeg videre. Jeg vandrer videre, til mine ben svigter, og jeg lægger mig ned og dør et sted, og til sidst når jeg den evige, stille havn, hvor der hverken er sorg eller suk...« tænkte fyrstinde Mária.
Men bagefter, når hun så sin far og især lille Koko (Nikolaj), svækkedes hendes forsæt. Hun græd stille og følte, at hun var en synder, der elskede sin far og sin lille nevø mere end Gud.

english.title: Book Six (1808 - 10) — Chapter 26
paragraphs: In the middle of summer Princess Mary received an unexpected letter from Prince Andrew in Switzerland, containing strange and surprising news. He wrote of his engagement to Natasha Rostova. The entire letter breathed a loving rapture for his betrothed and a tender, confiding affection for his sister. He wrote that he had never loved as he did now and that only now did he understand what life truly was. He asked his sister to forgive him for not having told her of his decision during his last visit to Bald Hills, though he had discussed it with their father. He had not told her for fear she would ask their father for his consent, angering the old man and bearing the brunt of his displeasure without achieving anything. "Besides," he wrote, "the matter was not so definite then as it is now. Our father insisted on a year's delay, and now already six months — half the time — have passed, and my resolve is firmer than ever. If the doctors did not keep me here at the spa I would be back in Russia already, but as it is I must postpone my return for three months. You know me and my relationship with Father. I want nothing from him. I have always been and always shall be independent; but to go against his will and provoke his anger, when he may remain with us only a short time longer, would destroy half my happiness. I am now writing to him about the same matter, and I beg you to choose a good moment to give him my letter and let me know how he takes it, and whether there is any hope that he may agree to shorten the waiting period by four months."
After long hesitation, doubt, and prayer, Princess Mary gave the letter to her father. The next day the old prince said to her quietly:
"Write and tell your brother to wait until I'm dead... It won't be long — I'll set him free soon enough."
The princess tried to reply, but her father wouldn't let her speak and, raising his voice higher and higher, cried:

"Marry, marry, my boy!... A fine family!... Smart people, eh? Rich, eh? Yes, a nice stepmother for little Nicholas! Write and tell him he can marry tomorrow if he likes. She'll be little Nicholas's stepmother, and I'll marry Bourienne!... Ha, ha, ha! He shouldn't be without a stepmother either! Only one thing — no more women in my house. Let him marry and live on his own. Maybe you'd like to go live with him too?" he added, turning to Princess Mary. "Go right ahead! Out into the cold... the cold... the cold!"

After this outburst the prince did not raise the subject again. But his suppressed fury at his son's weak-willed behavior found expression in his treatment of his daughter. To his former pretexts for mockery a new one was added — pointed references to stepmothers and conspicuous courtesies toward Mademoiselle Bourienne.
"Why shouldn't I marry her?" he asked his daughter. "She'll make a splendid princess!"

And lately, to her surprise and bewilderment, Princess Mary noticed that her father really was associating more and more with the Frenchwoman. She wrote to Prince Andrew about their father's reaction but tried to comfort him with hopes of a reconciliation.

Little Nicholas and his education, her brother Andrew, and religion were Princess Mary's joys and consolations; but besides these, since everyone must have personal hopes, Princess Mary had a hidden dream deep in her heart that provided the chief comfort of her life. This comforting dream and hope were given to her by God's folk — the half-witted wanderers and other pilgrims who visited her without the prince's knowledge. The longer she lived and the more she saw of life, the greater was her wonder at the shortsightedness of people who seek pleasure and happiness on this earth: toiling, suffering, struggling, and harming one another to attain an impossible, illusory, sinful happiness. Prince Andrew had loved his wife — she died, but that was not enough: he wanted to bind his happiness to another woman. Her father objected because he wanted a more distinguished and wealthy match for Andrew. And they all struggled and suffered and tormented one another and damaged their eternal souls, all for the sake of benefits that last no more than an instant. Not only do we know this ourselves, but Christ, the Son of God, came down to earth and told us that this life is but a moment, a trial; yet we cling to it and think to find happiness in it. "How is it that no one sees this?" thought Princess Mary. "No one except these despised holy wanderers who, with knapsack on their backs, come to me by the back door, afraid of being seen by the prince — not from fear of mistreatment but to save him from sin. To leave family, home, and all worldly cares, to wander in rough garments from place to place under an assumed name, doing no one any harm but praying for all — for those who drive one away as well as for those who shelter one: there is no life or truth higher than that!"

There was one pilgrim, a quiet, pockmarked little woman of about fifty named Theodosia, who for over thirty years had walked barefoot and worn heavy chains. Princess Mary was especially fond of her. Once, when they sat together in a dimly lit room before an icon, Theodosia was telling the story of her life, and the thought suddenly came to Princess Mary with overwhelming force that Theodosia alone had found the true path. She resolved then and there to become a pilgrim herself. She confided this idea to no one except her confessor, Father Akinfi the monk, who approved. Under the guise of a gift for the pilgrims, Princess Mary prepared a complete pilgrim's outfit for herself: a rough shirt, bast shoes, a coarse coat, and a black kerchief. Often, approaching the chest of drawers that held this secret treasure, Princess Mary would pause, wondering whether the time had come to put her plan into action.

Often, listening to the pilgrims' stories, she was so moved by their simple words — mechanical to them but full of deep meaning for her — that several times she was on the point of abandoning everything and running away from home. In her imagination she already saw herself beside Theodosia, dressed in coarse rags, walking with a staff and a knapsack on her back along a dusty road, making her way from one holy shrine to another, free from envy, earthly love, or desire, and reaching at last the place where there is no more sorrow or sighing, but eternal joy and bliss.

"I shall come to a place and pray there, and before I have time to get attached to it or love it, I shall move on. I will keep walking until my legs give way, and I'll lie down and die somewhere, and at last reach that eternal, peaceful haven where there is neither sorrow nor sighing..." thought Princess Mary.

But afterward, when she saw her father and especially little Koko — Nicholas — her resolve would weaken. She would weep quietly and feel that she was a sinner who loved her father and her little nephew more than she loved God.
